section.title: Samuel's Farewell
section.sectionRationale: With the king installed, Samuel steps back and gives his farewell as judge. He clears his own name, rehearses the LORD's saving history, and names again the sin of demanding a king. A thunderstorm in the dry season confirms his word, and the terrified people beg for prayer. Samuel answers with grace: though you have sinned, do not turn away; serve the LORD wholeheartedly, for He will not forsake His people for His name's sake, and I will not cease to pray for you. It is one movement: the last judge hands over to the monarchy with a call to fear the LORD.
section.thesis: Even as Israel's sin in demanding a king is exposed and confirmed by a sign from heaven, Samuel proclaims that the LORD, for the sake of His great name, will not abandon the people He was pleased to make His own, so that the way forward under a king is not despair but wholehearted fear of the LORD, sustained by a faithful intercessor.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Samuel clears his name before the LORD and His anointed, verses 1 to 5; the LORD's saving history and Israel's sin recounted, verses 6 to 15; the sign of thunder and the people's fear, verses 16 to 19; and the call not to turn away, grounded in God's faithfulness, verses 20 to 25.

units.label: Samuel clears his name
units.note: bear witness against me before the LORD and His anointed

verses.text: Then Samuel said to all Israel, “I have listened to your voice in all that you have said to me, and I have set over you a king.
Now here is the king walking before you, and I am old and gray, and my sons are here with you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day.

Here I am. Bear witness against me before the LORD and before His {{mashiach|anointed}}: Whose ox or donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated or oppressed? From whose hand have I accepted a bribe and closed my eyes? Tell me, and I will restore it to you.”
“You have not cheated us or oppressed us,” they replied, “nor have you taken anything from the hand of man.”
Samuel said to them, “The LORD is a witness against you, and His anointed is a witness today, that you have not found anything in my hand.” “He is a witness,” they replied.

units.label: The LORD's saving history and Israel's sin
units.note: the LORD your God was your king

verses.text: Then Samuel said to the people, “The LORD is the One who appointed Moses and Aaron, and who brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt.
Now present yourselves, so that I may confront you before the LORD with all the righteous acts He has done for you and your fathers.
When Jacob went to Egypt, your fathers cried out to the LORD, and He sent them Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place.
But they forgot the LORD their God, and He sold them into the hand of Sisera the commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hands of the Philistines and the king of Moab, who fought against them.
Then they cried out to the LORD and said, ‘We have sinned, for we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and Ashtoreths. Now deliver us from the hands of our enemies, that we may serve You.’
So the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel, and He delivered you from the hands of your enemies on every side, and you dwelt securely.
But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites was moving against you, you said to me, ‘No, we must have a king to rule over us,’ even though the LORD your God was your king.
Now here is the king you have chosen, the one you requested. Behold, the LORD has placed a king over you.

If you {{yare|fear}} the LORD and serve Him and obey His voice, and if you do not rebel against the command of the LORD, and if both you and the king who rules over you follow the LORD your God, then all will be well.
But if you disobey the LORD and rebel against His command, then the hand of the LORD will be against you as it was against your fathers.

units.label: The sign of thunder and the people's fear
units.note: the LORD sent thunder and rain

verses.text: Now, therefore, present yourselves and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes.
Is it not the wheat harvest today? I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain, so that you will know and see what a great evil you have committed in the sight of the LORD by asking for a king.”
So Samuel called to the LORD, and on that day the LORD sent thunder and rain. As a result, all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel.
They pleaded with Samuel, “Pray to the LORD your God for your servants so that we will not die! For we have added to all our sins the evil of asking for a king.”

units.label: The call not to turn away, grounded in God's faithfulness
units.note: the LORD will not abandon His people, for His great name's sake

verses.text: “Do not be afraid,” Samuel replied. “Even though you have committed all this evil, do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart.
Do not turn aside after worthless things that cannot profit you or deliver you, for they are empty.
Indeed, for the sake of His great {{shem|name}}, the LORD will not abandon His people, because He was pleased to make you His own.
As for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you. And I will continue to teach you the good and right way.
Above all, fear the LORD and serve Him faithfully with all your heart; consider what great things He has done for you.
But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away.”

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one, messiah. Samuel calls the newly anointed Saul the LORD's anointed and summons him as a witness. Even a flawed king bears this sacred title as God's designated ruler; the term keeps sounding through the book, building toward the true Anointed King, Christ, of whom every anointed one is a shadow.

yare.gloss: To fear, revere, stand in awe. The fear of the LORD is the heart of covenant loyalty, a reverent awe that leads to obedience and trust. Samuel makes it the one thing needful for king and people alike: fear the LORD, serve Him, and all will be well. It is not cringing dread but worshipful reverence that shapes a whole life.

shem.gloss: Name, reputation, revealed character. The LORD will not abandon His people for the sake of His great name; Israel's security rests not on their goodness but on God's commitment to His own honor and covenant. God saves and keeps His people so that His name, His known character as a faithful, saving God, is upheld before the world.

basic.context: Now that Saul is king, Samuel gives his farewell speech as the last judge. First he clears his own record: have I ever cheated or robbed any of you? No, they say. Then he retells Israel's history, how God saved them again and again, and how they still demanded a king even though the LORD was already their King. To drive the point home, Samuel calls on God to send thunder and rain in the dry wheat harvest, and God does, terrifying the people so that they beg for prayer. Samuel answers with astonishing grace: yes, you have sinned, but do not turn away from the LORD. Serve Him with all your heart, for He will not abandon His people for the sake of His great name, and I will keep praying for you. The question is: after such failure, is there hope? Yes, because God is faithful to His own name.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a covenant-renewal speech in the pattern of Moses and Joshua, holding together honest rebuke and real hope. It is not a promise that faithfulness always brings material blessing in a simple way; it lays out the covenant path of blessing and warning. The deepest note is grace: the ground of hope is not Israel's performance but God's commitment to His name. We should read it as a call to wholehearted fear of the LORD and as a revelation that God keeps His people for His own sake.
basic.originalLanguages: Samuel repeatedly calls Saul the LORD's mashiach, His anointed, the sacred title even a flawed king bears. He presses on king and people alike the one essential, to yare, to fear the LORD, a reverent awe that yields obedience and trust. And he anchors all hope not in their goodness but in God's shem, His great name: the LORD will not abandon His people for His name's sake, because He was pleased to make them His own.
basic.typology: Samuel, the blameless leader who intercedes for a sinful people and refuses to stop praying, foreshadows Christ, the sinless Mediator who ever lives to intercede. The covenant hope grounded in God's name, not human merit, points to the gospel, where God saves us for His own glory. And the anointed king who stands as witness anticipates the true Anointed King under whom all is finally set right.
basic.christ: Samuel can find no fault in his own conduct, and he stands and prays for a guilty people, refusing to cease interceding. He is a signpost to Jesus, the truly blameless One, who not only intercedes but bears the guilt Himself and ever lives to pray for us. The hope Samuel offers, that God will not forsake His people for His great name's sake, is secured in Christ, in whom God keeps and saves sinners to the praise of His glory. And the mashiach who stands as witness here points to the Anointed King who will never be swept away.
basic.god: God is the faithful covenant Lord who has saved His people again and again throughout their history. He is holy and just, sending the sign that exposes their sin. Yet He is astonishingly gracious: He will not abandon the people He was pleased to make His own, and He grounds their security in His own name rather than their record. He is the God who keeps His people for His own glory.
basic.crossReferences: Joshua 24 gives a parallel covenant-renewal farewell. Ezekiel 36 says God acts for the sake of His holy name, not Israel's merit. Romans 8 shows Christ interceding for His people. And Philippians 1 assures that God completes the good work He begins.
basic.oneStory: The last judge hands Israel over to the monarchy with honest rebuke and greater hope: God will not abandon His people for His name's sake. That promise, grounded in God's own glory rather than human faithfulness, runs through the whole story to Christ, the blameless Intercessor and true Anointed King, in whom God keeps and saves His people forever.

context.literary:
Chapter 12 is Samuel's formal farewell as judge, closing the transition to monarchy that began in chapter 8. It follows the pattern of covenant-renewal addresses like Joshua 24: a review of God's saving acts, an indictment, a call to obedience, and blessings and warnings. It marks the end of the era of the judges and sets the terms under which the monarchy must live.

The speech is shaped like a covenant lawsuit, the form Israel's later prophets use again and again, Micah 6:1-5, Isaiah 1:2-20, where the LORD calls witnesses, rehearses His past kindness, states the charge, and calls for a response. Samuel summons the LORD and His newly anointed king as witnesses against himself first, verses 3 to 5, before turning the same courtroom around to try the people, reciting a history of deliverance they cannot deny, verses 6 to 11, and naming their specific offense, verse 12. The out-of-season storm that follows functions much like the fire that answers Elijah on Carmel a generation later, a physical sign that settles an argument words alone could not.

The speech also closes the way it opened, with a summons to testimony, but the terms have shifted. It began with Samuel inviting the people to accuse him of wrongdoing and found him innocent; it ends with him warning that both the people and their king could yet be swept away for wrongdoing of their own, verse 25. The chapter frames the whole monarchy to come inside that same courtroom, blessing and curse compressed into two verses, 14 and 15, anticipating at far greater length the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28 to 30.
context.historical:
In Israel the wheat harvest fell in the dry season, when rain and thunderstorms were highly unusual, so the sign was unmistakably from God. A leader clearing his name before witnesses was a recognized way to hand over office with integrity. Samuel names past deliverers, Gideon, Barak, Jephthah, and himself, from the era of the judges.

The list of deliverers is not chosen at random. Jephthah had specifically saved Israel from the Ammonites, Judges 11:32-33, the very enemy Saul has just defeated at Jabesh-gilead in the previous chapter, so Samuel's history lesson lands with unusual force, the LORD has already proven, within living memory, that He can rescue Israel from this exact threat without a monarchy at all. Barak and Deborah answered the oppression of Sisera's army from Hazor, Judges 4 and 5, and Gideon, called Jerubbaal here after the name given him for tearing down Baal's altar, Judges 6:32, turned back the Midianites. Each deliverer arose from a different tribe and a different crisis, evidence that the LORD had never left His people without help.

Public covenant assemblies calling the nation to renewed obedience, complete with recited history and formal witnesses, were a known form of leadership transition in Israel, matched most closely by Joshua's farewell gathering at Shechem, Joshua 24:1, where the people likewise bound themselves to serve the LORD in the hearing of witnesses. Samuel, as Israel's last judge, hands over an office that has never before been passed to a king, and he marks the moment with exactly the same solemn form Israel already recognized.
context.canonical:
The chapter's teaching that God keeps His people for the sake of His name anticipates Ezekiel 36 and the New Testament gospel of grace. Samuel's ongoing intercession joins him to Moses as a great mediator, Jeremiah 15:1, and points forward to Christ's intercession. The conditional blessings and warnings frame the whole history of the monarchy in Samuel and Kings.

The Psalms remember Samuel by name for exactly the ministry this chapter displays, grouped with Moses and Aaron among those the LORD answered, Moses and Aaron were among His priests, Samuel was among those who called on His name, they called to the LORD and He answered them, Psalm 99:6. A worship book written generations later still praises Samuel for the very intercession he promises never to abandon in verse 23.

The verdict this chapter reaches on the monarchy, blessing if the king and people follow the LORD, sweeping away if they persist in evil, verses 14 to 15 and 25, is not the last word Scripture speaks on Israel's kings. Centuries later Hosea will look back on the whole institution and render a harsher summary, in My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away, Hosea 13:11, showing that Samuel's warning here was not rhetorical decoration but a real condition the monarchy would eventually fail to meet. The rejection language that first surfaced in chapter 8 and returned at Mizpah in chapter 10 reaches its fullest and most solemn statement here, closing an argument the book has been building since Israel first asked for a king.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
To close the age of the judges with an honest reckoning of Israel's sin in demanding a king, to set the covenant terms for life under the monarchy, and to ground the people's hope not in their own faithfulness but in God's commitment to His great name.

The author wants a reader standing at this hinge in Israel's history to feel the full weight of what has changed and what has not. Samuel's own integrity, publicly tested and publicly confirmed, verses 3 to 5, establishes that the era now ending was not a failure of leadership, the judges served Israel well, and God delivered through them repeatedly. What is ending is not competent government but a particular relationship, direct dependence on the LORD as king, and the writer wants that loss felt rather than glossed over, which is why the sign of thunder in the dry season is allowed to genuinely terrify the people rather than being softened.

At the same time the writer intends this farewell to function as the charter for everything Samuel and Kings will narrate afterward. By stating plainly the conditions under which the monarchy will stand or fall, verses 14 and 15, the author gives the reader a lens for judging every king to come, so that the collapse of the northern and southern kingdoms, when it eventually arrives, will read not as an unforeseen tragedy but as the fulfillment of terms Samuel spelled out here at the very start.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes Samuel's covenant address and a specific sign; it does not promise thunderstorms on demand or guarantee simple material reward for obedience. What endures is the call to wholehearted fear of the LORD, the warning against turning to worthless idols, and the assurance that God keeps His people for His name's sake.

Nobody today should expect a summoned storm to settle an argument, nor read verses 14 and 15 as a simple formula guaranteeing that obedient nations always prosper and disobedient ones always suffer immediately, since the historical books that follow will show plenty of complicated exceptions on both sides of that ledger. What does carry forward without qualification is the shape of the appeal itself, an honest naming of sin paired with a genuine call to return, and the conviction that God's people are kept not by a flawless record but by His own commitment to His name. Believers now stand in exactly the position Israel stood in then, forgiven and warned in the same breath, called to serve wholeheartedly not in order to earn God's favor but because they have already received more of it than they deserve.

debates.question: If asking for a king was such a great evil, why does Samuel still offer hope?

views.label: Grace grounded in God's name, not their merit
views.case: Samuel names the sin plainly, yet the ground of hope is God's own commitment: for the sake of His great name the LORD will not abandon the people He was pleased to make His own; hope rests on God's character, not on undoing the sin.

views.label: The path forward is repentance and wholehearted service
views.case: Though the request was evil, the people can still fear and serve the LORD from the heart; the covenant is not annulled, and genuine, ongoing faithfulness under the king remains open to them by God's mercy.

debates.bearing: Both hold together: sin is real and named, yet God's faithfulness to His name secures a future, calling His people to repent and serve rather than despair, a hope fully secured in Christ.

debates.question: What is the significance of Samuel's refusal to stop praying, verse 23?

views.label: Intercession as a sacred duty
views.case: Samuel regards ceasing to pray for the people as itself a sin against the LORD; the leader's task is to keep interceding and teaching the good way, so that pastoral care continues even after office is handed over.

views.label: A picture of the mediator God provides
views.case: Samuel's steadfast intercession models the mediating role that God graciously supplies for His people, pointing beyond himself to the great and permanent Intercessor, Christ.

debates.bearing: Either way the verse shows that God does not leave His people without a mediator to pray and teach, a mercy that finds its fullness in Jesus, who always lives to intercede.

study.originalLanguages:
Twice in this speech Samuel uses the very verb built into Saul's own name. The king you have chosen, the one you requested, verse 13, and later, we have added to all our sins the evil of asking for a king, verse 19, both render forms of sha'al, to ask, the root that gives Sha'ul, Saul, his name, asked for. Israel does not merely receive a king; it receives, by name, the walking answer to its own asking, a small irony Samuel never has to explain because the man standing beside him already carries it.

Samuel's repeated call to obey His voice, verse 14, and his warning against those who disobey the LORD, verse 15, both use forms of shama, the ordinary Hebrew verb for hearing, which in covenant contexts regularly does double duty as the verb for obedience. To hear the LORD's voice, in this idiom, is not merely to register sound but to act on it, the same assumption behind the great confession of Deuteronomy 6:4, hear, O Israel. Samuel is not asking Israel for polite attention; he is asking whether they will do what they have heard.

The verb see also threads through the speech, present yourselves and see this great thing, verse 16, and later, consider what great things He has done for you, verse 24, both built on ra'ah, to see, the same root behind roeh, the old word for a prophet as one who sees what others cannot. Samuel has spent his whole career seeing on Israel's behalf; here, in his farewell, he insists that Israel finally see for itself, in the plain evidence of an out-of-season storm, what it has refused to see through years of deliverance.

Finally, Samuel grounds Israel's future not in performance but in shem, name, God's revealed reputation and character, and in yare, the reverent fear that is covenant loyalty rather than terror. The pairing matters, the same chapter that records genuine pachad, dread, at the thunder, verse 18, calls Israel forward into a different and better fear, yare, one that leads to service rather than to paralysis, so that the emotional shock of the storm is meant to resolve into something steadier and more permanent than fright.

typology.type: The blameless leader who intercedes for a sinful people
typology.fulfillment: Samuel can invite the whole nation to accuse him and stand clean, then immediately turns to plead for the very people he has just indicted, refusing to let his integrity become distance from their guilt. Peter says of Christ, He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth, and yet He does not merely advocate from a safe distance, He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, 1 Peter 2:22-24, and now lives forever to intercede for those He died for, Hebrews 7:24-25. Samuel's innocence lets him pray for the guilty; Christ's innocence lets Him die for them.

typology.type: Covenant hope grounded in God's name, not human merit
typology.fulfillment: For the sake of His great name the LORD will not abandon His people, Samuel says, refusing to let their sin be the deciding factor in their future. Ezekiel will later put the same logic in God's own mouth, it is not for your sake that I will act, O house of Israel, but for My holy name, Ezekiel 36:22. Paul draws on the same well of grace for the gospel itself, that God presented Christ to demonstrate His own righteousness, Romans 3:25-26, so that in every era God's people are kept by His character, never by their record.

typology.type: The anointed king summoned as witness
typology.fulfillment: Saul stands beside Samuel as a living witness to Israel's innocence claim, a newly anointed king whose own reign will soon prove far from blameless. Revelation describes the rider on the white horse as Faithful and True, robed and named the Word of God, King of kings and Lord of lords, Revelation 19:11-16. Saul is summoned as a witness who will himself need forgiveness; the true Anointed King needs none, and He is the one before whom every other witness will finally be judged.

study.christ:
Samuel invites all Israel to name anything he has stolen, anyone he has cheated, and the assembly cannot find a single charge, verses 3 to 5. Scripture will only ever record one other perfectly clean defense of this kind, and it belongs to Jesus, who could ask His own accusers, which of you can prove Me guilty of sin, John 8:46, and receive a silence far less gracious than Israel's honest acquittal of Samuel. The difference is that Samuel's clean record only qualifies him to pray for the guilty; Christ's clean record qualifies Him to die in their place, bearing sins that were never His, 1 Peter 2:22-24.

Samuel then turns from his own innocence to Israel's history, reciting deliverance after deliverance the people had already half forgotten, and to their guilt, one clause, even though the LORD your God was your king, verse 12, exposing exactly what their request for a king had actually rejected. Every later king in Israel, at his best, is a stand-in for a Kingship Israel already had and traded away. Christ is the reversal of that trade, the true King who does not have to be requested because He comes offering Himself, and who receives, unlike Saul, a throne and a kingdom that will never end, Luke 1:32-33.

The storm Samuel calls down is a small, local sign meant to convict a single generation of a single sin. It anticipates the same authority the Gospels will record at the cross, where the sun was darkened over all the land, Luke 23:44-45, as if creation cannot stay silent when its Maker is dying at the hands of the very people He came to keep. Samuel's thunder proves a prophet right; the darkness at Calvary proves something far larger, that the true King was there being rejected and killed.

And Samuel's closing vow, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you, verse 23, is a mortal man's best attempt at a role only the immortal Mediator can fill without interruption. Hebrews says of Jesus that because He continues forever, He holds His priesthood permanently, and He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them, Hebrews 7:24-25. Samuel could only promise not to stop; Christ cannot stop, because He never dies.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God secure enough to let His own servant be publicly tested. Samuel does not simply assert his innocence, he opens himself to cross examination by an entire nation, and God lets that examination happen in full view, a small window into a Judge who does not need to rig the proceedings to protect the people He has appointed.

He is a God whose past kindness is a matter of public record rather than private feeling. Samuel does not appeal to Israel's memory of an abstract goodness, he lists names, Moses, Aaron, Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and specific rescues from specific enemies, because the LORD's faithfulness in this book is always concrete, tied to particular days and particular deliverances that anyone present could verify.

He is a God whose warnings are not bluster. The storm Samuel calls for arrives exactly when he says it will, in a season when everyone in that field knew such weather to be nearly impossible, so that the fear it produces is not manufactured but earned, evidence gathered in real time rather than a threat left to the imagination.

And He is, above every other thing this chapter shows, a God who refuses to let human failure be the last word on His relationship with His people. Israel has, by Samuel's own count, added a great evil to all its sins, and still He does not abandon them, not because their sin has become small in His eyes, He calls it evil twice, but because His own name, His revealed character as the God who keeps covenant, is now bound up with their future. Ezekiel will later say this almost as bluntly as Samuel does here, that God acts for His name's sake and not because Israel deserves it, a truth this chapter states first.

He is finally a God who provides intercession rather than leaving His people to face Him alone after such a failure. Samuel's vow never to cease praying is not merely a kind gesture from an old and generous man, it is the shape of how this God has always related to sinners who cannot yet stand in His presence unaided, through a mediator who pleads on their behalf, a pattern that will run through the whole of Scripture until it is fulfilled in a Mediator who never has to hand off the task to anyone else.

crossReferences.note: Joshua's own farewell gathers Israel, recites the LORD's saving acts from Abraham to the conquest, and calls the nation to choose whom it will serve. Samuel follows the identical pattern a generation later, proof that covenant renewal at a leader's departure was already a recognized and expected form in Israel.

It is not for your sake, O house of Israel, that I will act, but for My holy name. Ezekiel states, centuries later and at a far darker moment, the very principle Samuel already relies on here, that God's people are kept for the sake of His reputation, not their record.

Christ is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them. Samuel's vow never to cease praying for Israel is a mortal echo, offered for a lifetime, of the intercession Christ offers without end or interruption.

He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion. Paul's confidence answers the same fear that gripped Israel at the thunder in this chapter, that past failure might cancel a future with God, by grounding hope in God's follow-through rather than in human consistency.

Moses and Aaron were among His priests, and Samuel was among those who called on His name, they called to the LORD, and He answered them. A worship book written long after this chapter still remembers Samuel by name for the very intercession he promises here never to abandon.

He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth. Samuel's public acquittal, no one could find anything in his hand, is the closest human parallel Scripture offers before it describes a genuinely sinless Man who, unlike Samuel, used His innocence to bear the guilt of others rather than merely to intercede for them.

In My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away. Hosea's later verdict on the whole monarchy confirms that Samuel's conditional warning here, all will be well only if king and people follow the LORD, was not rhetorical caution but an accurate forecast of how the story would actually end.

Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is One, and you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart. Samuel's call to serve the LORD with all your heart, verse 20, deliberately echoes this foundational command, applying Israel's oldest confession to its newest and most uncertain arrangement, a king.

Darkness came over all the land, and the sun was darkened. The out-of-season storm that terrifies Israel into recognizing its sin at Samuel's word is answered, centuries later, by a far greater sign in the sky, marking not an old request for a king but the death of the King every request had always been pointing toward.

study.oneStory:
Every farewell in Scripture marks a hinge, and this one marks one of the largest in the whole Old Testament, the last time Israel will be led directly by a judge raised up as each crisis demanded rather than by a hereditary throne. From here forward the story runs through kings, faithful ones rare, faithless ones common, until both the throne and the temple lie in ruins and Israel sits in exile asking whether the promises made at moments like this one still hold.

Samuel's speech answers that question before it is even asked. He does not pretend the request for a king was harmless, and he does not pretend the monarchy will fix what was actually broken, the people's own wandering heart. What he offers instead is a hope with a much sturdier foundation than any king could provide, the LORD will not abandon His people, for His great name's sake, a promise that does not depend on Israel getting government right, because Israel never fully does, not under judges, not under kings, not even under the best of them.

That promise is what carries the story through everything that follows this chapter, the divided kingdom, the exile Hosea will describe as God taking back in wrath what He gave in anger, and the long silence before a King finally comes who cannot be swept away because He never sins in the first place. Samuel's vow to keep praying, never repeated by any single successor for long, finds its permanent fulfillment in a Priest who lives forever to intercede, so that the very weakness this chapter exposes, no leader stays faithful indefinitely, becomes the reason the story needs, and gets, a King who does. The last judge hands Israel forward not to a solution but to a long wait that ends, at last, in Christ.

quiz.q: What did Samuel establish at the start of his farewell?

options.text: His own integrity, that he had never cheated, oppressed, or taken a bribe from anyone.
options.note: Verses 3 to 5; Samuel clears his record before the LORD and His anointed.

options.text: That he had installed a king over Israel as they asked.
options.note: He did say this, but the pointed opening was clearing his own name of any wrongdoing.

options.text: That his sons would rule after him.
options.note: The opposite; he had stepped aside and a king now ruled, not his sons.

options.text: That he had grown rich from his years of leadership.
options.note: He proved he had taken nothing; he had not enriched himself.

quiz.q: What sign confirmed Samuel's word about the evil of asking for a king?

options.text: God sent thunder and rain during the dry wheat harvest, when such storms never came.
options.note: Verses 16 to 18; the out-of-season storm was unmistakably from God.

options.text: A sudden storm frightened the people.
options.note: True, but the key was that it came in the dry harvest season, proving it was from God.

options.text: An earthquake shook the assembly.
options.note: The sign was thunder and rain, not an earthquake.

options.text: Fire fell from heaven on an altar.
options.note: The sign here was thunder and rain in the dry season, not fire.

quiz.q: On what did Samuel ground Israel's hope after their sin?

options.text: On God's commitment to His own great name, since He was pleased to make them His own.
options.note: Verse 22; hope rests on God's faithfulness to His name, not Israel's record.

options.text: On the people serving the LORD with all their heart.
options.note: Samuel calls for this, but the ground of hope he names is God's own name and pleasure.

options.text: On Saul proving to be a faithful king.
options.note: Hope rested on God's faithfulness, not on the king, who is also warned.

options.text: On Israel earning back God's favor by good works.
options.note: The hope is grounded in God's grace and name, not in earning favor.

quiz.q: How did Samuel respond to the frightened, repentant people?

options.text: He told them not to turn away but to serve the LORD wholeheartedly, and vowed never to stop praying for them.
options.note: Verses 20 to 23; grace, a call to fear the LORD, and steadfast intercession.

options.text: He urged them to serve the LORD with all their heart.
options.note: True, but omits his gracious reassurance and his vow to keep praying for them.

options.text: He told them their sin was beyond forgiveness.
options.note: The opposite; he offered real hope grounded in God's faithfulness.

options.text: He abandoned them and refused to pray.
options.note: He said it would be sin to cease praying for them.

quiz.q: How does Samuel's farewell point forward to Christ?

options.text: The blameless leader who intercedes and never ceases to pray foreshadows Christ, the sinless Mediator who ever lives to intercede.
options.note: Hebrews 7:25; Samuel's integrity and prayer point to Jesus, who also bears our guilt.

options.text: He shows that leaders should pray for the people they serve.
options.note: True, but it stops short of Christ, the great Intercessor Samuel foreshadows.

options.text: He teaches that God's people can never fall away.
options.note: Samuel warns they can be swept away if they persist in evil; hope rests on God's grace.

options.text: He has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The blameless intercessor and the hope grounded in God's name clearly point to Jesus.

questions: Samuel could invite anyone to accuse him and stand clean. Could those who know you best testify to your integrity in money, power, and honesty?
Israel kept forgetting the LORD's past deliverances and reaching for their own solutions. What great things has God done for you that you are tempted to forget?
Samuel grounded hope not in Israel's goodness but in God's great name. How does resting your security on God's faithfulness rather than your performance change the way you face your failures?
Samuel said it would be sin to stop praying for the people. Who has God given you to intercede for, and are you faithful to keep praying for them?
Above all, Samuel said, fear the LORD and serve Him with all your heart. What would it look like this week to let a reverent awe of God shape your whole life?

translationNotes.note: Jerubbaal is Gideon, Judges 6:32; the BSB follows the Septuagint and Syriac in reading Barak and Samuel, where the Hebrew has Bedan and some texts read Samson, all judges God raised up to deliver Israel.
The clause even though the LORD your God was your king names the heart of the sin: they had a King already.
For the sake of His great name, shem, the LORD will not abandon His people; Israel's security rests on God's commitment to His own honor, echoed in Ezekiel 36:22-23.
